summary: Describes how a Push Notification Service can wake a suspended SIP user agent, and how the UA can send binding-refresh REGISTER requests and receive requests while suspended. It defines new SIP URI parameters to exchange push service information. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: A sleeping phone app can be woken by a message from a notification service when a call arrives.

questions: how do sip push notifications work
what is the sip 555 response code
subtitle: How a SIP proxy uses a phone's push notification service to wake a sleeping app for calls and registration refreshes.

tldr.problem: Mobile operating systems suspend idle apps, so a suspended SIP user agent cannot send its periodic REGISTER refreshes or receive incoming SIP requests.
tldr.mechanism: The user agent hands its push token to a SIP proxy in new URI parameters on its Contact URI. The proxy asks the Push Notification Service to wake the app, the app sends a binding-refresh REGISTER, and only then does the proxy forward the held request.
tldr.outcome: A suspended SIP client can still receive calls and keep its registration alive, at the cost of extra delay while the push and REGISTER complete.

facts.label: Recommended push lead time
facts.value: At least 120 seconds before binding expiry

today: RFC 8599 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2019, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It also creates an IANA "PNS" subregistry for pn-provider values.

sections.title: The Problem of Suspended Apps
sections.content:
To save battery, devices and operating systems suspend applications that are not in use. A suspended app may not wake itself with timers and may not be woken by incoming network traffic. A Push Notification Service (PNS) exists to wake such an app: other applications ask it to send a message, called a push notification, to a user application.

For a SIP user agent (UA) this is a real problem. While suspended it cannot send binding-refresh REGISTER requests, cannot receive incoming SIP requests, and cannot keep connections alive with keep-alives, for example with the SIP Outbound mechanism in RFC 5626. The RFC says typical examples are the Apple Push Notification service (APNs) on Apple iOS and Firebase Cloud Messaging (FCM) on Android, and that some PNSs follow the standard in RFC 8030 while others are proprietary.
sections.plainLanguage: An app that is napping cannot hear anything. Phones have a special wake-up service that can poke a sleeping app, and this RFC teaches SIP to use it.

sections.title: The Push Flow and the PRID
sections.content:
When a UA registers with a PNS it receives a unique Push Resource ID (PRID). The format depends on the PNS, and how to find the PNS and register with it is outside the scope of this RFC. The UA gives the PRID to a SIP proxy in a REGISTER request.

Later, when the proxy gets a request for a new dialog or a standalone request (such as INVITE or MESSAGE) for that UA, or decides the UA must refresh its binding, it sends a push request carrying the PRID to the PNS. The PNS wakes the UA, the UA sends a binding-refresh REGISTER, and the proxy forwards it to the registrar. The proxy then forwards the held request using normal SIP routing.

The proxy MUST be in the signaling path of the UA's REGISTER requests and of requests forwarded toward the UA by the proxy responsible for the UA's domain. The REGISTER also creates any NAT bindings the incoming request needs to reach the UA.
sections.plainLanguage: The app gets a secret ticket number from the wake-up service and gives it to a helper. When a call comes, the helper shows the ticket, the service pokes the app, and the app tells everyone where to find it.

sections.title: New URI Parameters and Indicators
sections.content:
The PNS details travel in four SIP URI parameters: pn-provider (the type of PNS), pn-param (extra details for the provider), pn-prid (the PRID) and pn-purr (used for long-lived dialogs). The meaning of pn-prid and pn-param depends on the pn-provider value.

Feature-capability indicators carried in Feature-Caps headers announce support: sip.pns (a type of PNS is supported), sip.vapid (the proxy supports VAPID, with its public key as the value), sip.pnsreg (the minimum time in seconds before expiry the UA must refresh) and sip.pnspurr (carries the PURR). A UA that can wake itself adds a sip.pnsreg media feature tag to its Contact.

Three providers are defined: apns (pn-param is the Team ID and Topic, pn-prid is the device token), fcm (pn-param is the Project ID, pn-prid is the registration token) and webpush for RFC 8030 (pn-param MUST NOT be used, pn-prid is the push subscription URI).
sections.plainLanguage: The app writes the ticket number and which wake-up service it uses onto its address label. Special stickers tell everyone what each side can do.

sections.title: User Agent Behavior
sections.content:
To ask for push notifications, the UA MUST put pn-provider, pn-prid and, if the PNS needs it, pn-param in the Contact URI of its REGISTER. If the 2xx response has a Feature-Caps header with a matching sip.pns value, a proxy will request pushes. Without it, the UA MUST NOT assume pushes will come.

Whenever the UA receives a push notification it MUST send a binding-refresh REGISTER with the same pn-* parameters, and one for each binding it has. It can ignore any push payload, since this RFC defines no use for one. To stop pushes, the UA SHOULD remove its binding and MUST NOT include pn-prid in that REGISTER.

For privacy, the UA MUST NOT put these parameters (except pn-purr) in non-REGISTER requests, so the PNS information does not reach the remote peer. A UA that can refresh by its own timer adds the sip.pnsreg tag, and must still refresh on every push.

A UA can also query the network: a REGISTER with pn-provider but no pn-prid gets back the supported PNS types, or a 555 response if none is supported.
sections.plainLanguage: When the app is poked, it wakes up and says again where it lives. It never shows its secret ticket number to the people it calls.

sections.title: Proxy Behavior and the Push Bucket
sections.content:
A proxy that supports the UA's PNS type MUST advertise it with sip.pns in the REGISTER before forwarding it, and again in the 2xx response. It MUST send a 423 (Interval Too Brief) or skip push handling if the binding would expire before it could trigger a refresh. It is RECOMMENDED that it requests a push at least 120 seconds before a binding expires. A proxy that knows no proxy toward the registrar supports the PNS MAY answer with the new 555 (Push Notification Service Not Supported) response.

When a request arrives for the UA, the proxy stores it in the SIP Request Push Bucket and starts a Bucket Timer. When the REGISTER 2xx response arrives with a Contact whose pn-* parameters match the stored Request-URI, the proxy removes the request from the bucket and forwards it. Waiting for the 2xx confirms the registrar accepted the UA and that it may receive messages for that URI.

If the REGISTER fails or the push request fails, the proxy SHOULD or MUST send an error, with 404 or 480 RECOMMENDED. If the timer expires it MUST send 480. The RFC warns this adds delay, which matters for non-INVITE requests, and notes test results during development showed the REGISTER typically arrived around 2 seconds after the push request.
sections.plainLanguage: The helper puts your call in a basket, pokes the app, and hands the call over only when the app has checked in. If the app never answers, the helper tells the caller it is not available.

sections.title: Long-Lived Dialogs and Replaces
sections.content:
Mid-dialog requests do not carry the pn-* parameters, so a different mechanism is needed for long-lived dialogs such as those using SIP event notification. The proxy stores the push information when it sees the initial REGISTER and creates a PURR (Proxy Unique Registration Reference) as a key to find it. It returns the PURR in a sip.pnspurr indicator.

The UA that wants pushes for mid-dialog requests MUST put that PURR in a pn-purr parameter in the Contact of the initial dialog request or its 2xx response. The proxy adds itself to the route with Record-Route, so mid-dialog requests come back through it, and then uses the bucket as before.

To stop client fingerprinting, the proxy MUST periodically generate a new PURR, while keeping old values that have ongoing dialogs. A PURR must be unforgeable, anonymous and unlinkable to entities other than the proxy. The same PURR mechanism supports the SIP Replaces header from RFC 3891.
sections.plainLanguage: For a long phone call the helper keeps a locker with the ticket inside and gives the app a locker key that changes now and then, so nobody can track it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security of any particular PNS is out of scope. Typically the PNS requires the requesting proxy to be authenticated and authorized. If it does not, someone who obtains the parameters from SIP signaling could trigger pushes, which drains the UA's battery and causes unnecessary SIP traffic. The VAPID mechanism in RFC 8292 lets a proxy identify itself to the PNS with a signed token, so devices can restrict pushes to that proxy's public key.

Operators MUST secure SIP signaling, and TLS MUST be used unless another mechanism with strong crypto properties is known to protect it. They MUST also ensure the PNS parameters are not sent to other users or untrusted entities, including through the registration event package in RFC 3680, where subscriptions MUST be authenticated and authorized.
sections.plainLanguage: If a stranger learns your ticket number, they could keep poking your app and wear out your battery. So the numbers are kept private and the lines are locked.
